This oil deal with Venezuela is absolutely insane.

President Trump just announced that the US has reached a deal to secure "majority control" of over 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.

Furthermore, the US currently has ~46 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves.

Combined with the 65 billion barrels covered by this agreement, the US would have domestic reserves plus control over ~111 billion barrels of oil.

To put this into perspective, the entire world has roughly 1.57 TRILLION barrels of proven crude oil reserves.

In other words, the US is set to control ~7.1% of all proven oil reserves in the world under this new agreement with Venezuela.

At ~111 billion barrels, the US would be almost exactly in-line with the United Arab Emirates, which has 113 billion barrels of proven crude reserves, and it would exceed Kuwait's 102 billion barrels.

Assuming the agreement is structured as outlined in President Trump’s announcement, the implications for global energy markets will be enormous.

We will publish more in-depth analysis soon.

Martin Casado on why artificial intelligence is the wrong term and why a16z's new fund is called the Machine Age Fund:

"Artificial intelligence was the wrong word. It's machine intelligence... because it's not how humans think. It is a cache of human thought."

"To date, we don't know how to take an AI with no knowledge and put it out in the world and have it reconstruct language. That's not what we've done. We've built something that can learn off of everything we've already learned and then use that in a productive way."

"AI is a general term that goes back 70 years in computer science formally that applies to many different things, and of course it's got a lot of baggage. Either from science fiction or from you know, Nick Bostrom who wrote about it."

"You want to emphasize the machine part of it... You've really come to a place where you pour money into something and then you're limited by the actual machines below it. It's a nod to the hardware component is so significant in this wave, and we want to acknowledge that."

@martin_casado @eriktorenberg

BREAKING: US M2 money supply surged +$102.8 billion in July, to a record $23.22 trillion.

This marks the 27th consecutive monthly increase.

Since the start of 2026, M2 has now risen +$862.7 billion.

Furthermore, money supply now stands $1.43 trillion above the March 2022 peak.

Since 2000, money in circulation has grown at an average annual rate of +6.3%, or ~$700 billion a year.

US money creation is expanding at a rapid pace.

Raghu Raghuram and Ben Horowitz say a billion knowledge workers are just one of the next AI demand waves:

"ChatGPT went from a casual app to coding for professionals. Now, using coding, you now built amazing tools for knowledge workers. So that's the next frontier. And now there are over a billion knowledge workers."

"Progressively, each of these things unlocks an order of magnitude more demand, and we are just at the start of this."

"And now you have Grok Bot. What happened with coding is kind of happening with all use of computer via Grok Bot, and so we're in a whole 'nother wave of demand, and most certainly there's gonna be more to come."

"It does seem quite unlimited at the moment, and we haven't even gotten into embodied AI or robots, which are gonna be another source of demand."

@RaghuRaghuram @bhorowitz

tweets.text:
Wheat prices are surging.

US wheat futures jumped +6.4% on Wednesday and +1.3% on Thursday, to $7.58 per bushel, the highest level since July 2023.

Wheat prices have risen +19% so far this month, and are up +50% since the start of 2026.

This comes amid growing concerns about further disruptions to grain-export ports and terminals along Ukraine's and Russia's Black Sea coast.

Russia and Ukraine together account for more than 25% of global wheat exports, while also supplying significant amounts of global barley, corn, and sunflower oil exports.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's agricultural exports in the 2026-27 season are now expected to be 29.6 million tons, or -54% lower than the previous estimate of 64.4 million tons, according to its agriculture ministry.

Another wave of food inflation may be on its way.

Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, and Ben Horowitz on what the hyperscalers can see that others can't, and why they're going to spend a trillion dollars on it:

"The demand for AI is basically infinite, and as a result of that, every part of the supply chain is under duress. Everything, including materials used to make things like memory."

" Even the business model of the AI wave is really putting a lot of stress on the existing systems because they weren't built for AI, they weren't built for those workloads."

"If you look at the hyperscalers, their CapEx spend has been exploding. Next year, supposedly it's gonna reach a trillion dollars collectively. This year it's about $700 billion."

"They see demand from everywhere... If anybody has visibility, it is them... On the demand side, the signals have never been clearer."

"If you look at the supply across the board, it's basically all booked out to 2028. It's so bad, we've actually seen multi-day auctions for a few thousand GPUs."

@martin_casado @RaghuRaghuram @bhorowitz @eriktorenberg

Oil sits at $82 and looks calm. The war is hiding in the freight bill.

Shipping a supertanker of crude from Saudi Arabia to China just hit a record $647,000 a day, more than 10x a year ago. Moving one cargo through the Strait of Hormuz now runs about $20 million, because few owners will risk the passage and the ones who will are charging for it.

This is a price shock in the plumbing of the oil market while the barrel stays calm. Houthi attacks are pushing Saudi crude the long way around Africa, adding 30 days a voyage, and traders are swapping cargoes ship-to-ship outside Hormuz to dodge the danger.

Calm crude with tanker rates at records means the market is pricing the detour and betting the war stays contained. If Hormuz actually closes, the shock jumps from the freight line to the barrel, and $82 is the last cheap print you get.

Almost 3 years since the Red Sea attacks began, and global shipping still hasn't gone home.

🚢 Cape of Good Hope: ~108 transits/day — still double its pre-2023 norm 
🚢 Suez Canal: 46/day — recovering (+33% YoY) but ~40% below pre-crisis levels

The detour became the default. And now the region's shipping stress has a second front: since March, our Hormuz index shows transits through the strait down 93% vs. its long-run norm.

Tracked live via our real-time chokepoint transit indices — daily vessel counts for 11 global chokepoints, updated hourly on the terminal.

The revaluation strategy backed by the threat of tariffs has already failed spectacularly. In my view, the decisive reason was that the Trump administration folded first in its trade war with Beijing, with American stores at one point essentially running out of goods.

As a Beijing policy advisor told me a year ago, “We missed the best chance to shift China toward a more consumption-oriented growth model because the US proved too weak (怂).”

Now that China has successfully weathered what was arguably the most aggressive trade war with the US—and its trade surplus continues to surge— I see little reason to believe that tariff threats can force Beijing to rebalance its economy. If anything, the experience may have reinforced the opposite lesson in Beijing: the US lacks the leverage to force China to change its economic model.
